I've been farming here in Quzhou for over thirty years, and I've learned not to get clever with the land. I've got eight mu, and every year I plant winter wheat after the autumn harvest and follow it with summer maize as soon as the wheat comes off in June. That's the system my father used, and it's the system every household around here uses, because the North China Plain gives us just enough heat and frost-free days to squeeze in two crops if you don't waste time between them.

For wheat, I'll buy improved seed from the supply shop in town — probably Jimai or something similar, whatever they recommend this year. I'll rotary till the field after the corn stubble is chopped, spread my base fertilizer, and drill the seed before the soil gets cold. Come spring, I'll irrigate four times: once to help it through winter if it's dry, once at jointing, once at heading, and once during grain filling. I'll topdress with urea when the wheat starts moving in March. Two rounds of spray should handle the weeds and the bugs — I'm not going to spend extra money on more chemicals than that.

For the summer maize, I'll plant hybrid seed the same day the wheat comes out of the field — every day you delay costs you yield. Maize is less work than wheat in some ways. I'll irrigate twice, maybe three times if July is scorching, and I'll put down fertilizer at planting and side-dress at the big trumpet stage. Two pesticide passes: one for weeds right after emergence, and one for corn borers later on. Rotary tillage again — it's fast and my neighbor's tractor does a good job.

I don't grow vegetables or anything else on a large scale. Eight mu isn't much, and splitting it up means buying different machines, learning different markets, and taking risks I can't afford. Wheat and maize have buyers who come to the village. I know the price won't make me rich, but it pays for my son's school fees and the old tractor repairs. I expect about 500 jin per mu of wheat and maybe 600 jin per mu of corn if the weather holds.
